name: Green tea (Camellia sinensis) leaf extract
lead: Green tea leaf extract is a concentrate of polyphenols, mainly catechins such as epigallocatechin gallate (EGCG), from unoxidized Camellia sinensis leaves. It is used in topical skincare as an antioxidant and in oral supplements.[1]

Wikipedia reports that human clinical research has not found good evidence of benefit for most health claims, and that a 2011 European Food Safety Authority (EFSA) review judged most proposed claims, including some about skin protection from UV damage, not sufficiently supported.[1] Oral extracts have been associated with liver toxicity, mainly attributed to EGCG, and Health Canada recommended warning labels in 2017.[1]
infobox: Topical ointment approved in US (2006) for genital warts

paras: Green tea polyphenols include EGCG, epicatechin gallate and other flavonoids. Brewed green tea is almost all water; extracts sold as supplements can contain up to about 17% caffeine by weight.[1]
In cosmetics, green tea extract is promoted as an antioxidant and soothing ingredient. In 2006 the US FDA approved a topical green tea extract ointment as a prescription drug for genital warts.[1]

Wikipedia summarizes randomized trials of green tea for non-appearance outcomes: small reductions in blood pressure (about 2 to 3 mm Hg), lower total and LDL cholesterol in a 2013 Cochrane meta-analysis, and no good evidence for weight loss.[1] No trials specific to appearance outcomes are summarized there, and EFSA found its skin-protection claims not sufficiently supported.[1]

Excess consumption, especially of extracts, has been associated with liver toxicity and rarely liver failure. EFSA reported that long-term intake of extracts above 800 mg EGCG per day raised liver enzymes in some people and could not establish a safe dose; Health Canada (2017) recommended a warning label and use by adults only.[1] A 2020 Cochrane review listed gastrointestinal effects, raised liver enzymes and, rarely, skin reactions as possible adverse effects of extracts.[1] Green tea interferes with the cancer drug bortezomib.[1]

timeline.event: US FDA approves a topical green tea extract ointment as a prescription drug for genital warts.[1]
EFSA review finds most green tea health claims not sufficiently supported.[1]
Health Canada recommends a liver-related warning label for green tea extracts.[1]

card.summary: Catechin-rich antioxidant botanical common in skincare; general health claims lack strong support and oral extracts carry liver warnings.
card.note: Oral extracts linked to liver toxicity; evidence here is from a single encyclopedia summary.

quick.overview:
Green tea extract concentrates the polyphenols of green tea leaf and is used in creams, serums and supplements as an antioxidant.

Reviews summarized on Wikipedia found insufficient evidence for most claims, though one topical form is an approved prescription for genital warts.
quick.mechanism: Catechins such as EGCG are antioxidants; no proven biological effects in humans are stated for them in the source.
quick.risks: Extracts, especially oral, have been linked to liver injury; EFSA could not set a safe dose. Rare skin reactions are reported.
